title: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine's Mission to the Great Khan
intro: Pope Innocent IV sent the Franciscan Giovanni da Pian del Carpine as papal legate to the Great Khan of the Mongol Empire, partly in protest at the Mongol invasion of Christendom and partly to learn the Khan's intentions and military strength. He carried a letter from the Pope.
ending: Güyük Khan refused to become Christian and demanded that the Pope and the rulers of Europe come and swear allegiance to him. Giovanni brought the Khan's letter back to the Pope at Lyon and later wrote the Ystoria Mongalorum, the oldest European account of the Mongols.

stops.text: Giovanni set out from Lyon, where the Pope then resided, on Easter day. He was sixty-three and bore the Pope's letter to the Great Khan. Stephen of Bohemia travelled with him.
stops.quote: "At the age of sixty-three Carpini embarked from Lyon," where the Pope then resided, on Easter day (16 April 1245), accompanied by another friar, Stephen of Bohemia

stops.text: Stephen of Bohemia broke down at Kaniv, near Kiev, and was left behind. Giovanni and his interpreter, the Franciscan Benedict of Poland, entered the Tatar posts here and went on towards the Don and Volga.
stops.quote: Stephen of Bohemia, who broke down at Kaniv near Kiev and was left behind.

stops.text: After leaving Batu's camp on the Volga on Easter day, the envoys rode across the steppe and reached the imperial camp called Sira Orda, near Karakorum. They had ridden an estimated 3,000 miles in 106 days.
stops.quote: on the feast of St Mary Magdalene (22 July), they reached the imperial camp called Sira Orda (Yellow Pavilion), near Karakorum and the Orkhon River.

stops.text: The friars witnessed the formal enthronement of Güyük at another camp nearby, the Golden Ordu, and were then presented to the new emperor. Güyük refused to become Christian.
stops.quote: On 24 August, they witnessed the formal enthronement at another camp in the vicinity called the Golden Ordu, and they were then presented to the new emperor.

stops.text: The Khan dismissed the expedition in November, and the friars made a long winter journey home, often lying on the bare snow. They reached Kiev, where Slavonic Christians welcomed them with festive hospitality.
stops.quote: They reached Kiev on 10 June 1247. There and on their further journey, the Slavonic Christians welcomed them as risen from the dead with festive hospitality.

stops.text: The travellers crossed the Rhine at Cologne on their way to the Pope.
stops.quote: Crossing the Rhine at Cologne, they found the Pope still at Lyon and delivered their report and the Khan's letter.

stops.text: They found the Pope still at Lyon and delivered their report and the Khan's letter.
stops.quote: they found the Pope still at Lyon and delivered their report and the Khan's letter.

notes: Wrocław is placed before Kaniv by geography; the article tells Stephen's breakdown at Kaniv first, then Benedict joining at Wrocław, so the order is the editor's reading. Batu's ordu on the Volga (early April 1246, the two fires) is left out: the article names no town, only the river. The Syr Darya cities and the Dzungarian lakes are not named towns. Sira Orda and the Golden Ordu are both camps near Karakorum; both use the Karakorum point (entry karakorum), which is approximate. The article names the second Easter as 8 April 1246 for leaving Batu. Dates for Wrocław, Kaniv, Cologne and Lyon (return) are years only; 1245 for the outward stops and 1247 for the return are inferred from the surrounding narrative. Kiev is only named on the outward route in passing, so only the return is a stop. The article gives the Khan's dismissal as November (1246 by context).
